summary: Awilix is an interactive web platform for exploring and comparing candidate landing sites at the Moon’s south pole. We developed a visual browser that brings lunar mission data together in one place, so users can examine terrain, compare locations side by side and understand what makes each site valuable. It addresses the challenge by making complex lunar data accessible to mission planners, students and the general public, rather than leaving it locked in technical datasets. The project matters because the south pole is the focus of the next era of lunar exploration. Its permanently shadowed craters may hold water ice, and nearby ridges receive near-constant sunlight, making the region ideal for sustained human presence. Choosing where to land is one of the most consequential decisions in any mission, and Awilix helps people explore those options clearly and confidently.
details:
Awilix lets users browse lunar south pole landing sites and compare them side by side, turning scattered mission data into one clear, searchable experience. Instead of digging through separate datasets, users explore each site visually and quickly see how locations differ. The benefits are clarity, speed and accessibility: experts can weigh options efficiently, while students and curious members of the public can understand lunar science without specialist training. Our intended impact is to widen public engagement with the next era of Moon exploration and support better-informed discussion about where humanity should land.

We built the project with TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS, supported by linting and automated tests, and deployed it. No special hardware is required, so it works in any modern browser.

The project is creative in its space-themed interface, adapted from a Figma community design, and in its identity. It is named after Awilix, the K’iche’ Maya moon goddess and queen of the night, linking modern exploration to the Moon’s cultural heritage. Along the way, our team considered data accuracy, performance, responsive design, ease of use for newcomers, and proper credit for our sources.
